say: Welcome, everyone; over the next 50 minutes we'll use four fictional workbooks to move from scattered business data to a recommendation we can defend. We'll explore sales, marketing, customer experience and new products before bringing the evidence together in one conversation.

The twelve prompts give us a route through the work, not a set of answers to memorize. Your job is to check what Copilot says against the files and decide what deserves to survive into the final recommendation.
welcome.ask: Which part of a launch recommendation would you most want to verify before spending money?
welcome.watch: Use the page's 50-minute framing and stage allocations: setup 4, sales 7, marketing 6, customer 6, product 7 and combined analysis 10 minutes.

say: Here's the rhythm we'll keep throughout the workshop: get the right workbook, copy the exact prompt, run it in the application shown, and inspect the evidence. Copying rather than retyping lets us spend our attention on the business question instead of fixing missing words.

When we reach a verification screen, a tick means you've actually looked at the relevant data. Different answers can be useful, but a confident paragraph without a checked row isn't enough to move the decision forward.
needs.ask: What would you need to see in a workbook before you were comfortable ticking a verification check?
needs.watch: Point to the Download, Copy, Run and Verify cards; distinguish the workshop illustration from the learner's live workbook and Copilot response.

say: If a download fails, try it again or use the ZIP, and if copying fails, select the prompt text and copy it yourself. Those are practical recovery steps, not reasons to change the exercise or the underlying data.

If Copilot is slow or unavailable, let me know so we can choose how to continue without inventing a result. If your wording looks different from a neighbor's, check the workbook instead of repeatedly asking for the same sentence.
help.ask: If two answers use different wording but cite the same checked evidence, what should we compare?
help.watch: Demonstrate manual copying only if needed; keep unresolved availability issues visible and never supply a fabricated response to unlock progress.

say: Download Regional Sales and Distribution, Marketing Performance, Customer Experience and New Product Exploration into one folder so we can find them again later. Keep their original filenames and worksheet names, and leave the raw data unchanged throughout the exercise.

Each file gives us a different part of the launch decision, so missing one will matter when we combine the evidence. If an individual link doesn't work, use the ZIP containing the same four workbooks rather than substituting your own business data.
get.ask: Can you locate all four original workbooks together before we open the sales file?
get.watch: Keep downloads within the 4-minute setup allocation; confirm four files, not four copies of one file, and use the ZIP fallback when needed.

say: Before our first prompt, open Regional Sales and Distribution in Excel and make sure you can open its Copilot pane. Keep Copilot Chat available in a separate browser tab, because we'll change tools when the four files need to be considered together.

Now check that all four files are downloaded and that the first workbook is actually open, rather than just visible in a folder. Tick each readiness item only when it's true, and tell me which item is holding you up if you can't continue.
ready.ask: Which readiness item, if any, is still preventing you from running the first sales prompt?
ready.watch: The readiness gate shows 2 minutes within setup; check all four items and avoid Reset my progress unless the learner deliberately wants to clear existing ticks.

say: Our first sales prompt asks for the commercial picture across transactions, targets, distributors and returns, not simply a list of the biggest sales figures. We're looking for underperformance, margin pressure, unusual discounts and distribution concerns, with the market, product, channel and numbers attached.

Copy this prompt into Copilot in the sales workbook and let it finish before judging the response. As you read, notice whether a concern is supported by the records or is only a possible explanation, because those deserve different levels of confidence.
t1ado.ask: Which sales finding would become less attractive if you also considered its margin or return pattern?
t1ado.watch: Allow 4 minutes for 1A including its verification; keep learners in Regional Sales and Distribution.xlsx and do not reveal any record-specific findings before inspection.

say: Let's test one of those sales claims by opening the supporting worksheet and comparing the actual figures with the response. Check that Copilot has used more than one sheet and has treated sales performance and margin performance as different questions.

For the distributor check, inspect D017 in Distributors and read its fulfilment, return-rate and status fields without assuming what they'll show. Only tick the relevant boxes after you can explain which row supports a finding and which part remains an interpretation.
t1aok.ask: What did the D017 row let you confirm, and what would still require an explanation beyond the file?
t1aok.watch: Use the remainder of 1A's 4 minutes; have learners read D017's fields themselves and verify at least one distributor or return-related risk.

say: Now we'll turn the sales analysis into three comparisons: net sales against target by market, net sales by category and channel, and gross margin percentage over time. The prompt asks Copilot to choose chart types, create Sales Analysis, and explain what each visual helps us notice.

Run it in the same workbook and look for a chart that makes a business pattern easier to discuss than the raw rows did. Keep an eye on the units, because a visual can look convincing while comparing local currencies or margin measures in an unhelpful way.
t1bdo.ask: Which of these three comparisons would help you explain the most important sales concern to a colleague?
t1bdo.watch: Allow 3 minutes for 1B and verification; look for Sales Analysis without assuming worksheet creation succeeded.

say: Open Sales Analysis if it was created and inspect the labels before accepting the story the charts appear to tell. Check the market comparison against sales and targets, the category-and-channel comparison against its rows, and the time view against Gross Margin Percentage.

Different local currencies need appropriate separation or a clear warning rather than an unexplained direct comparison. If the worksheet wasn't created, record Copilot's explanation honestly, and use the checks to distinguish an actual visual from a suggestion for one.
t1bok.ask: Which label, unit or currency check most changed how you read one of the sales charts?
t1bok.watch: Stay within 1B's 3-minute allocation; verify Gross Margin Percentage rather than Gross Margin Local and ask for one row-backed chart observation.

say: If you're comfortably on track, this optional prompt asks Copilot to look for duplicate or near-duplicate sales records and explain which fields make them suspicious. It's a review list with transaction IDs, not permission to remove records that happen to look similar.

Stay in Sales Transactions and compare the fields on any records it lists before deciding whether the similarity matters. If you're behind, skip this challenge and keep your attention on the required evidence checks, because completing the main decision is more important than adding another search.
opt1.ask: Which matching fields would make a pair of sales records worth investigating rather than automatically deleting?
opt1.watch: Optional only, with no extra time allocation; inspect listed transaction IDs after the response and leave every source record unchanged.

say: Switch to Marketing Performance, where the question is whether attention turns into commercial results. This prompt brings together campaign activity, digital engagement, events and audience information to compare spending with leads, redemptions, attributed sales and event orders.

Run it and look for an explanation of the relationship between those measures, rather than praise for the largest click count. We want to understand where apparent success deserves a closer look and where comparisons between channels need a qualification.
t2ado.ask: What evidence would convince you that a busy campaign produced commercial value rather than just attention?
t2ado.watch: Allow 3 minutes for 2A including verification; confirm Marketing Performance.xlsx is open and keep digital and tasting-event evidence in scope.

say: Choose a marketing finding and follow it back to spending and either attributed sales or orders within 30 days. Then inspect CMP022 and compare its engagements, clicks, leads and attributed sales, rather than treating any one of those numbers as the whole outcome.

Check that the response also used Events and Tastings, since the exercise isn't limited to digital activity. Before ticking the checks, identify a limitation in attribution or comparability so the recommendation doesn't claim more than the files support.
t2aok.ask: What can you confirm from CMP022's figures, and which comparison needs an attribution caveat?
t2aok.watch: Complete within 2A's 3 minutes; use CMP022 as the public verification target without supplying its values or a predetermined conclusion.

say: The next prompt asks who might be a sensible audience for an unfamiliar premium beverage, not simply which segment is largest. Its visualization compares premium interest, experimentation, price sensitivity, audience size, category preference and market before recommending segments and marketing channels.

Run it in the marketing workbook and read the recommendation as a combination of audience fit and route to reach them. Notice whether a large audience is genuinely qualified for this launch, or whether interest and willingness to experiment point us somewhere else.
t2bdo.ask: What trade-off would you accept between a larger audience and stronger premium interest with lower price sensitivity?
t2bdo.watch: Allow 3 minutes for 2B and verification; require a market, segment and channel rather than an audience-size ranking alone.

say: Find the recommended audience in Audience Segments and compare the interest, experimentation and price-sensitivity fields with the visual. We should be able to explain why that audience suits the launch, not just repeat the order of a chart.

Check that the response names a market, segment and preferred channel, and that audience size hasn't crowded out the other evidence. If you can't trace the recommendation to the segment rows, leave the check open and ask for the missing support.
t2bok.ask: Which Audience Segments fields support the recommended channel and which make you cautious about the audience?
t2bok.watch: Use the remainder of 2B's 3 minutes; verify the actual segment rows and avoid equating premium interest with a completed purchase.

say: Open Customer Experience and ask Copilot to connect feedback, profiles, service cases and product preferences. We're looking for recurring positive themes and complaints, differences between markets or segments, and places where written comments don't fit the numeric ratings.

Run the prompt and keep both kinds of evidence in view, because a rating alone won't explain what the customer described. Ask whether a theme repeats across records or is just one example, and whether a service or distributor issue changes the product story.
t3ado.ask: When a written comment and its rating point in different directions, what should we investigate before summarizing it?
t3ado.watch: Allow 3 minutes for 3A including verification; keep Customer Experience.xlsx open and do not announce the feedback contradiction in advance.

say: For this check, inspect FB0041 in Customer Feedback and compare Overall Rating, the component ratings and Written Comment. Let the fields show you whether there's a contradiction rather than trying to make the record fit Copilot's wording.

Then test another theme against its supporting records and look for a service or distributor pattern beyond product sentiment. The checks are asking whether the response uses comments and numbers responsibly and separates recurring themes from isolated examples.
t3aok.ask: What does comparing FB0041's comment with its ratings add that the overall rating alone would miss?
t3aok.watch: Stay inside 3A's 3-minute allocation; learners inspect FB0041 themselves and identify the distinction between a repeated theme and one unusual record.

say: Now we're asking which customers could be realistic early adopters, using sensory preferences alongside purchasing potential. The prompt compares sweetness, smokiness, smoothness, alcohol range, acceptable price, experimentation, premium purchase ratio and interest in new products across markets and segments.

Run it and look for a recommendation that combines willingness to try something unfamiliar with evidence of premium purchasing. A segment saying it likes new products is useful context, but we still need to understand what it likes and what price range it accepts.
t3bdo.ask: Which combination of experimentation, premium purchasing and price preference would make an early-adopter segment credible?
t3bdo.watch: Allow 3 minutes for 3B and verification; keep sensory fit, acceptable price and purchasing evidence together.

say: Follow the recommended segment into Customer Profiles and Product Preferences and compare the fields that support its early-adopter profile. Check that both experimentation and premium purchasing matter, with sensory preferences and acceptable price ranges named clearly.

Look at the visual's market or segment labels so you know whose preferences you're reading. Before ticking the checks, remove any leap from interest in new products to guaranteed demand, because the recommendation needs to stay within what these rows actually tell us.
t3bok.ask: Which supporting row helps distinguish a curious customer segment from one with realistic premium purchasing potential?
t3bok.watch: Finish within 3B's 3 minutes; ask learners to open both Customer Profiles and Product Preferences rather than verify only the summary.

say: Open New Product Exploration and compare the proposed products across concepts, sensory results, sourcing and market opportunity. This prompt asks whether appeal can become a viable product-market choice once pricing, costs, minimum orders, supply capacity and distribution readiness are considered.

Run it and look for a named product-market pair with both a reason to pursue it and a constraint to manage. We aren't selecting the best-tasting entry in isolation; we're testing how the customer-facing appeal fits the commercial and operational evidence.
t4ado.ask: Which operational constraint could outweigh an otherwise attractive sensory profile for a launch?
t4ado.watch: Allow 4 minutes for 4A and verification; confirm all four worksheets are considered and keep costs, supply and market fit in the discussion.

say: Take a recommended product-market pair and trace it across Product Concepts, Sensory Panel, Sourcing Assessment and Market Opportunity. Compare expected price with recommended retail price, then check the capacity, minimum-order and lead-time evidence that could affect execution.

Ask whether the response has explained the trade-off instead of automatically choosing the highest sensory score. Tick only what you've inspected, and keep the major commercial constraint beside the recommendation so it isn't lost when we combine the files.
t4aok.ask: Which checked cost, price or supply field most affects your confidence in the recommended product-market pair?
t4aok.watch: Use the remainder of 4A's 4 minutes; confirm a product and market are named and verify operational fields in Sourcing Assessment.

say: Our sensory comparison puts all six proposed products side by side, from Aurelius Oak through Ember Coast. The prompt asks for visuals of smoothness, aroma, sweetness, smokiness, fruitiness, spiciness, overall score, purchase intent and expected price, followed by an explanation of broad versus specialist appeal.

Run it and look at how the measures are displayed before deciding which profile looks strongest. We want a useful positioning discussion, not a single blended score that hides different scales or treats every strong flavor as universally desirable.
t4bdo.ask: Which sensory comparison would help explain a specialist product without calling it universally better or worse?
t4bdo.watch: Allow 3 minutes for 4B and verification; ensure all six products remain in the comparison and watch for misleading mixed measurement scales.

say: Check whether the visual distinguishes broad appeal from specialist appeal without mixing sensory scores, prices and purchase intent misleadingly. For Black Fjord, inspect the evidence behind the specialist interpretation rather than assuming smokiness must be good or bad for everyone.

Choose a sensory outlier and compare Overall Score with Purchase Intent and the other fields that matter to that record. If the response hasn't checked inconsistencies, make that need explicit before ticking the box, and trace one visual observation back to the source.
t4bok.ask: What evidence makes a sensory outlier a positioning question, a data-quality question, or both?
t4bok.watch: Stay within 4B's 3 minutes; verify Black Fjord's specialist assessment and an outlier without supplying a fixed answer or undisclosed evaluation ID.

say: We're moving from individual workbook analysis to one connected conversation in Copilot Chat. Type a slash, search for each original filename and select Regional Sales and Distribution, Marketing Performance, Customer Experience and New Product Exploration in that same chat.

Look for all four attachments before sending the first combined prompt, because separate conversations won't give this exercise the shared evidence we're asking for. Tick each file check only when you can see it attached, and keep this conversation for the remaining prompts.
attach.ask: Can you see all four original workbooks attached to this one Copilot Chat conversation?
attach.watch: The attachment gate shows 2 minutes; demonstrate slash-search and selection, then confirm four attachment chips before exposing the combined prompt.

say: The first combined prompt asks Copilot to build an evidence base across all four attached files before recommending anything. It connects existing sales, marketing-channel results, sensory preferences, service or distribution risks and viable product concepts, with workbook and worksheet references for every major finding.

Run it in this chat and read for the boundary between confirmed evidence, calculation, possible explanation and missing information. If the response sounds smooth but hides where a claim came from, that claim isn't yet ready to support our decision.
t5ado.ask: Which cross-file finding needs two source checks before you would use it in the recommendation?
t5ado.watch: Allow 3 minutes for 5A including verification; keep the four attachments in the same conversation and require source names for major findings.

say: Check that the response actually references all four workbooks rather than stitching together unsupported summaries. Choose one cross-file claim, open both underlying sources, and compare the values or preferences that are being connected.

Now look for a contradiction or missing input and make sure it hasn't been silently turned into a fact. Tick the evidence checks only after you can say which part is directly supported and which part is a calculated interpretation or possible explanation.
t5aok.ask: What changed when you checked the same cross-file claim against both underlying workbooks?
t5aok.watch: Finish within 5A's 3 minutes; ask for two underlying source checks on one connected claim, not just four filenames in the answer.

say: With the evidence base in place, ask for the three strongest new product-market combinations and the reasons alternatives were selected or rejected. The prompt brings together current sales and channels, marketing effectiveness, customer and sensory fit, price, costs, supply, distribution, growth, competition and sourcing risk.

Run it in the same chat and look for an actual comparison of trade-offs, not three independent endorsements. Each choice needs more than one workbook behind it, and an attractive score may still leave a product unsuitable to launch now.
t5bdo.ask: Which trade-off should determine the ranking when customer appeal and operational readiness disagree?
t5bdo.watch: Allow 3 minutes for 5B and verification; require exactly three product-market combinations with comparison and rejection or deferral reasoning.

say: Count the recommendations first: there should be exactly three product-market combinations, with commercial, customer and operational support for each. Then compare how the response ranks them and explains an alternative that was rejected or deferred despite an attractive score.

Open the underlying rows for one recommendation and check that the explanation reaches beyond a single workbook. If you can only find sensory support, for example, leave the commercial or operational claim unconfirmed until its evidence has been checked.
t5bok.ask: Which checked constraint explains why one attractive alternative was rejected or deferred?
t5bok.watch: Use the remainder of 5B's 3 minutes; separate the required three recommendations from additional alternatives discussed as rejected or deferred.

say: Now ask for low, base and high first-year revenue scenarios for each recommended product-market combination. The prompt requires visible formulas using customers, conversion, purchase frequency, units, price and supply constraints, with source values distinguished from assumptions the files don't provide.

Run it and treat the range as something to inspect, not a promised result. We need to see how the numbers were assembled and what had to be assumed before a forecast deserves space in the final recommendation.
t5cdo.ask: Which forecast input would you be most uncomfortable accepting without a clearly labeled assumption?
t5cdo.watch: Allow 2 minutes for 5C including verification; check all three combinations receive scenarios and do not supply invented conversion rates or prices.

say: Pick one scenario and follow the displayed calculation so another person could reproduce how its revenue was estimated. Check that the source values can be found in the attached workbooks and that any missing conversion, frequency or other input is labeled as an assumption.

Compare forecast units with available supply and look for an explicit warning if the scenario goes beyond it. Before ticking the checks, identify the major uncertainty and remove any false precision that makes the forecast sound more certain than its inputs.
t5cok.ask: Which assumption or supply check most widens your view of the low-to-high revenue range?
t5cok.watch: Stay within 5C's 2 minutes; verify one calculation and source input, then confirm low, base and high scenarios and visible supply constraints.

say: Our last prompt asks Copilot to act as a skeptical commercial director and challenge the recommendation we've just built. It should look for unsupported assumptions, contradictory evidence, data-quality problems, execution risks and reasons the revenue forecast could fail, then revise the proposal or confidence where needed.

Run it without defending the earlier answer simply because we spent time producing it. A useful critique gives us specific reasons to change or qualify the decision, rather than a polished repetition of the same recommendation.
t5ddo.ask: Which part of the recommendation would you most want a skeptical reviewer to challenge?
t5ddo.watch: Allow 2 minutes for 5D and verification; remain in the existing chat so the critique addresses the actual recommendation and scenarios.

say: Compare the critique with the earlier proposal and find a weakness that genuinely affects the decision or its confidence. Check that a data-quality concern is distinguished from a business risk, because those call for different kinds of follow-up.

Look for a reasoned revision and the information still needed before a real investment decision, then verify a claim against the attached rows. If the critique merely repeats the proposal, don't treat that as proof we've challenged it successfully.
t5dok.ask: What did the critique change or qualify, and what evidence explains that change?
t5dok.watch: Complete within 5D's 2 minutes; ask learners to identify an actual confidence revision or justified qualification and a remaining information need.

say: Copy the empty recommendation table and fill its three priority rows with the product-market combinations your checked evidence supports. For each, include the target segment, support from sales, marketing, customer and product data, revenue scenarios, main risk and an honest confidence level.

Use the latest critique to decide what to retain or change rather than pasting the earlier answer untouched. This table is our decision artifact: someone else should be able to see both why an option is attractive and what still makes it uncertain.
final.ask: Which risk and confidence level would you put beside your highest-priority combination, and why?
final.watch: Use the closing time without adding a new exercise allocation; copy the blank table, replace placeholders and retain all seven columns for three priorities.

say: This pack contains the exact prompts we've used, so you can copy one you want to keep or download the whole set. Think about which business question helped you most, whether that was separating attention from outcomes, checking customer contradictions or challenging a forecast.

The useful thing to take away isn't an unverified answer from today's fictional files. It's a prompt paired with the habit of checking its evidence, so when you reuse the approach you still know what needs to be inspected.
pack.ask: Which exact prompt will you keep, and which evidence check will you carry with it?
pack.watch: Show individual Copy and whole-pack download; distinguish the twelve main prompts from the optional duplicate-record challenge included in the pack.

say: We've moved from four separate workbooks through exploration and visuals to a connected recommendation, scenarios and a deliberate challenge. The important progress is being able to explain what the files support, not just getting Copilot to produce an impressive-looking answer.

Keep the three habits from this workshop: check the rows, label assumptions and keep the decision with people. Before we finish, choose one prompt you'll reuse and name the evidence you'd check before acting on its response.
learned.ask: Which prompt will you reuse this week, and what will you verify before trusting its output?
learned.watch: Close within the 50-minute session; invite one concrete reuse example and acknowledge unfinished checks rather than presenting them as completed.
